Fortran objects behind a Qt window

Created with Grok Build

Source code by Jonas Lindemann, from the oop_fortran repository.

The particle program is the same Fortran style as the shape classes, with the call direction reversed from the Fortran-calls-C++ example. ParticleSystem and ParticleSimulation are derived types with private data and type-bound procedures. A Fortran module holds one of each and publishes bind(C) procedures. The C++ window never sees a particle array. It calls those procedures, and paintEvent draws whatever they return.

Each section shows the procedure, then what it does. A procedure that computes a position, a radius, a time step, a collision, or a color has the formula next to the lines that implement it.

Qt Widgets 6.8.2 supplied the window. The clip below is that window, recorded on this machine while the pointer used Pause, the scaling slider, and Update.

mf_datatypes¶

mf_datatypes.f90
module mf_datatypes

use iso_fortran_env

implicit none

integer, parameter :: dp = real64
integer, parameter :: sp = real32
integer, parameter :: ik = int32
real(dp), parameter :: pi = 3.141592653589793238462643383279502884197_dp

end module mf_datatypes

dp is real64, sp is real32, and ik is int32. pi is the double constant used when a random direction becomes a velocity. This is separate from the bar program’s mf_datatypes. The names match. The contents differ. Each program compiles the copy that sits in its own directory.

π=3.141592653589793238462643383279502884197\pi = 3.141592653589793238462643383279502884197π=3.141592653589793238462643383279502884197
(1)

That literal is the value of pi. The velocity loop multiplies by it.

mf_utils¶

This copy is a smaller printer than the bar program’s copy. It has no integer matrix printer and no integer edit code.

mf_utils.f90
interface print_matrix
    module procedure print_matrix_d, print_matrix_s
end interface

interface print_vector
    module procedure print_vector_d, print_vector_s
end interface

interface rand_mat
    module procedure rand_mat_d, rand_mat_s
end interface

interface rand_vec
    module procedure rand_vec_d, rand_vec_s
end interface

integer, private :: field_width = 10
integer, private :: field_decimals = 4
character :: field_code(1) = 'G'

The defaults are width 10, decimals 4, and real edit descriptor G.

set_print_format¶

mf_utils.f90
subroutine set_print_format(width, decimals, code)

    integer, optional :: width
    integer, optional :: decimals
    character, optional :: code(1)

    if (present(width)) then
        field_width = width
    end if

    if (present(decimals)) then
        field_decimals = decimals
    end if

    if (present(code)) then
        field_code = code
    end if

end subroutine set_print_format

A present width, decimal count, or one-character code replaces the matching variable. There is no integer-code argument. The particle window never calls this subroutine. The console driver does not call it either. particle_interface uses the module, which is why the file is on the link line.

print_matrix_d and print_matrix_s¶

mf_utils.f90
subroutine print_matrix_d(A, name)

    real(dp), intent(in) :: A(:,:)
    character(*), intent(in), optional :: name
    integer :: rows, cols, slen
    integer :: i, j
    character(255) :: fmt
    character(255) :: sfmt

    rows = size(A,1)
    cols = size(A,2)
    slen = len_trim(name)

    if (slen<10) then
        write(sfmt, '(A,I1,A)') '(TL1,A,A',slen,',A,I3,A,I3,A)'
    else if (slen<100) then
        write(sfmt, '(A,I2,A)') '(TL1,A,A',slen,',A,I3,A,I3,A)'
    else
        write(sfmt, '(A,I3,A)') '(TL1,A,A',slen,',A,I3,A,I3,A)'
    end if

    if (cols<10) then
        if (field_width<10) then
            write(fmt, '(A,I1,A,I1,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        else
            write(fmt, '(A,I1,A,I2,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        end if
    else if (cols<100) then
        if (field_width<10) then
            write(fmt, '(A,I2,A,I1,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        else
            write(fmt, '(A,I2,A,I2,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        end if
    else
        if (field_width<10) then
            write(fmt, '(A,I3,A,I1,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        else
            write(fmt, '(A,I3,A,I2,A,I1,A)') '(', cols, field_code, field_width, '.', field_decimals, ')'
        end if
    end if

    !write(*,'(TL1,A)') repeat('-', cols*field_width)
    print*,''
    if (present(name)) then
        write(*,sfmt) 'Matrix ',trim(name),' (',rows, ' x ', cols, ') DP'
    else
        write(*,'(TL1,A,I3,A,I3,A)') 'Matrix (',rows, ' x ', cols, ') DP'
    end if
    write(*,'(TL1,A)') repeat('-', cols*field_width)


    do i=1,rows
        write(*,fmt) (A(i,j), j=1,cols)
    end do

    write(*,'(TL1,A)') repeat('-', cols*field_width)

end subroutine print_matrix_d

These build a G format the same way the bar printer does. The title ends in DP or SP. With the defaults and four columns the data format is (4G10.4). Nothing in the particle program calls them.

The random helpers and init_rand¶

mf_utils.f90
subroutine rand_mat_d(A, randMin, randMax)

    real(dp), intent(inout) :: A(:,:)
    real(dp), intent(in) :: randMin, randMax

    call random_number(A)

    !    min ---- max

    A = randMin + (randMax-randMin) * A

end subroutine rand_mat_d

random_number fills the array with U∈[0,1)U \in [0, 1)U∈[0,1), and the next statement scales it:

A=amin⁡+(amax⁡−amin⁡) UA = a_{\min} + (a_{\max} - a_{\min})\, UA=amin​+(amax​−amin​)U
(2)

A = randMin + (randMax-randMin) * A is that formula. The particle system does not call rand_mat_d. It calls random_number itself and scales the radii with the same expression, written out in particle_system_init.

mf_utils.f90
subroutine rand_mat_s(A, randMin, randMax)

    real(sp), intent(inout) :: A(:,:)
    real(sp), intent(in) :: randMin, randMax

    call random_number(A)

    !    min ---- max

    A = randMin + (randMax-randMin) * A

end subroutine rand_mat_s

subroutine rand_vec_d(a, randMin, randMax)

    real(dp), intent(inout) :: a(:)
    real(dp), intent(in) :: randMin, randMax

    call random_number(a)

    !    min ---- max

    a = randMin + (randMax-randMin) * a

end subroutine rand_vec_d

subroutine rand_vec_s(a, randMin, randMax)

    real(sp), intent(inout) :: a(:)
    real(sp), intent(in) :: randMin, randMax

    call random_number(a)

    !    min ---- max

    a = randMin + (randMax-randMin) * a

end subroutine rand_vec_s

rand_mat_s, rand_vec_d, and rand_vec_s are the same scaling for the other ranks and kinds.

mf_utils.f90
subroutine init_rand()
    integer :: values(1:8), k
    integer, dimension(:), allocatable :: seed
    real(real64) :: r
    call date_and_time(values=values)
    call random_seed(size=k)
    allocate(seed(1:k))
    seed(:) = values(8)
    call random_seed(put=seed)
end subroutine

init_rand seeds the generator from the millisecond field values(8). The local r is declared and never used. The particle system calls init_random_seed in particle_utils instead of this subroutine.

init_random_seed¶

particle_utils.f90
module particle_utils

        use mf_datatypes

        implicit none

contains

subroutine init_random_seed

        integer :: values(1:8), k
        integer, dimension(:), allocatable :: seed
        real(dp) :: r

        call date_and_time(values=values)

        call random_seed(size=k)
        allocate(seed(1:k))
        seed(:) = values(8)
        call random_seed(put=seed)

end subroutine init_random_seed

end module particle_utils

particle_utils has this one subroutine. It reads date_and_time into an eight-element integer array, asks random_seed how long the seed is, and fills every seed element with values(8), the millisecond field. The generator is then seeded from that array. Two starts in the same millisecond get the same sequence. The local r is declared and never used.

particle_system_init calls this once, before it draws positions and radii.

ParticleSystem¶

particle_classes.f90
type ParticleSystem
private
    integer(ik) :: m_n_particles
    real(dp) :: m_v0
    real(dp) :: m_rmin
    real(dp) :: m_rmax
    real(dp) :: m_dt
    real(dp), pointer :: m_pos(:,:)
    real(dp), pointer :: m_vel(:,:)
    real(dp), pointer :: m_r(:)
contains
    procedure :: init            => particle_system_init
    procedure :: destroy         => particle_system_destroy

    procedure :: print           => particle_system_print
    procedure :: write_sizes     => particle_system_write_sizes
    procedure :: write_positions => particle_system_write_positions

    procedure :: count           => particle_system_count
    procedure :: v0              => particle_system_v0
    procedure :: set_v0          => particle_system_set_v0
    procedure :: rmin            => particle_system_rmin
    procedure :: set_rmin        => particle_system_set_rmin
    procedure :: rmax            => particle_system_rmax
    procedure :: set_rmax        => particle_system_set_rmax
    procedure :: dt              => particle_system_dt
    procedure :: positions       => particle_system_positions
    procedure :: velocities      => particle_system_velocities
    procedure :: radius          => particle_system_radius

    procedure :: particle        => particle_system_particle
    procedure :: particle_count  => particle_system_particle_count

end type

The type is the box of particles. Everything is private: the count, the speed m_v0, the radius limits, a time step m_dt that init never sets, and three pointers. m_pos is (n,2)(n, 2)(n,2), m_vel is (n,2)(n, 2)(n,2), and m_r is (n)(n)(n). They are pointers so the accessors can hand the caller a pointer to the same memory.

The bindings are the methods. init, destroy, print, write_sizes, and write_positions change or report the whole set. count, v0, rmin, rmax, dt, positions, velocities, and radius are the readers. set_v0, set_rmin, and set_rmax are the writers. particle and particle_count are the two the C++ window uses on every frame.

particle_system_init¶

particle_classes.f90
subroutine particle_system_init(this, n, rmin, rmax, v0)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    integer(int32), intent(in) :: n
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: rmin
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: rmax
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: v0

    integer(ik) :: i
    real(dp) :: alfa

    this % m_n_particles = n
    allocate(this % m_pos(n,2))
    allocate(this % m_vel(n,2))
    allocate(this % m_r(n))

    if (present(v0)) then
        this % m_v0 = v0
    else
        this % m_v0 = 0.001_dp
    endif

    if (present(rmin)) then
        this % m_rmin = rmin
    else
        this % m_rmin = 0.005_dp
    endif

    if (present(rmax)) then
        this % m_rmax = rmax
    else
        this % m_rmax = 0.015_dp
    endif

    call init_random_seed()

    call random_number(this % m_pos)
    call random_number(this % m_r)

    do i=1,this % m_n_particles
        call random_number(alfa)
        alfa = 2.0_dp*pi*alfa
        this % m_vel(i,1) = this % m_v0 * cos(alfa)
        this % m_vel(i,2) = this % m_v0 * sin(alfa)
    end do

    this % m_r = this % m_rmin + this % m_r * (this % m_rmax - this % m_rmin)

end subroutine particle_system_init

The count is required. The radius limits and the speed are optional. Missing values become

Got function '\min' with no arguments as subscript at position 23: ….001, \qquad r_\̲m̲i̲n̲ ̲= 0.005, \qquad…

v_0 = 0.001, \qquad r_\min = 0.005, \qquad r_\max = 0.015

which are the numbers in the window’s text fields and in the three else branches.

The subroutine allocates the three arrays, seeds the generator, and fills m_pos and m_r with random_number. Positions land in the unit square because random_number returns values in [0,1)[0, 1)[0,1). The window draws that square.

Each particle then gets a speed of v0v_0v0​ in a random direction. random_number(alfa) draws u∈[0,1)u \in [0, 1)u∈[0,1), and the next three lines are

α=2πu,vx=v0cos⁡α,vy=v0sin⁡α\alpha = 2\pi u, \qquad v_x = v_0 \cos\alpha, \qquad v_y = v_0 \sin\alphaα=2πu,vx​=v0​cosα,vy​=v0​sinα
(4)

alfa = 2.0_dp*pi*alfa overwrites the uniform draw with the angle. m_vel(i,1) and m_vel(i,2) are vxv_xvx​ and vyv_yvy​. The speed of every particle is v0v_0v0​, because cos⁡2α+sin⁡2α=1\cos^2\alpha + \sin^2\alpha = 1cos2α+sin2α=1.

The radius line scales the unit draw already stored in m_r:

Got function '\min' with no arguments as subscript at position 7: r = r_\̲m̲i̲n̲ ̲+ u\,(r_\max - …

r = r_\min + u\,(r_\max - r_\min)

this % m_r = this % m_rmin + this % m_r * (this % m_rmax - this % m_rmin) is that formula, applied to the whole array at once. A particle is not kept inside the square by this subroutine. The simulation does that later, and only by flipping a velocity.

particle_system_destroy¶

particle_classes.f90
subroutine particle_system_destroy(this)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this

    deallocate(this % m_pos, this % m_vel, this % m_r)
    this % m_n_particles = -1

end subroutine

Deallocates the three arrays and sets the count to -1. The window calls the C wrapper of this from the MainWindow destructor, and again when Update builds a new system.

particle_system_print¶

particle_classes.f90
subroutine particle_system_print(this)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    integer(ik) :: i

    print *, 'Max particle x coord = ', maxval(this % m_pos(:,1))
    print *, 'Min particle x coord = ', minval(this % m_pos(:,1))
    print *, 'Max particle y coord = ', maxval(this % m_pos(:,2))
    print *, 'Min particle y coord = ', minval(this % m_pos(:,2))

end subroutine particle_system_print

Prints the maximum and minimum of each coordinate, maxval and minval of the two columns of m_pos. Neither driver calls it. The integer i is declared and never used.

particle_system_write_sizes and particle_system_write_positions¶

particle_classes.f90
subroutine particle_system_write_sizes(this)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    integer(ik) :: i

    open(unit=15, file='particle.state', access='APPEND')
    write(15, '(I10)') this % m_n_particles
    do i = 1,this % m_n_particles
            write(15, '(2F12.5)') this % m_r(i)
    end do
    close(unit=15)

end subroutine particle_system_write_sizes

subroutine particle_system_write_positions(this)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    integer(ik) :: i

    open(unit=15, file='particle.state', access='APPEND')
    write(15, '(I10)') this % m_n_particles
    do i = 1,this % m_n_particles
            write(15, '(2F12.5)') this % m_pos(i,:)
    end do
    close(unit=15)

end subroutine particle_system_write_positions

Both open particle.state with ACCESS='APPEND', write the count as an integer of width 10, write one record per particle, and close the file.

write_sizes writes m_r(i) with format (2F12.5). The output list has one real, so each radius record is one F12.5 number. write_positions writes m_pos(i, :), which is two reals, so each position line has xxx and yyy in two F12.5 fields.

The console driver is what calls these. The window calls run_iteration, which does not write the file.

Readers and writers¶

particle_classes.f90
real(dp) function particle_system_v0(this) result(v0)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this

    v0 = this % m_v0

end function

subroutine particle_system_set_rmin(this, rmin)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    real(dp), intent(in) :: rmin

    this % m_rmin = rmin

end subroutine

subroutine particle_system_set_rmax(this, rmax)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    real(dp), intent(in) :: rmax

    this % m_rmax = rmax

end subroutine

subroutine particle_system_set_v0(this, v0)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    real(dp), intent(in) :: v0

    this % m_v0 = v0

end subroutine

real(dp) function particle_system_rmin(this) result(rmin)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this

    rmin = this % m_rmin

end function

real(dp) function particle_system_rmax(this) result(rmax)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this

    rmax = this % m_rmax

end function

real(dp) function particle_system_dt(this) result(dt)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this

    dt   = this % m_dt

end function

function particle_system_positions(this) result(arr)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    real(dp), pointer :: arr(:,:)

    arr => this % m_pos

end function

function particle_system_velocities(this) result(arr)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    real(dp), pointer :: arr(:,:)

    arr => this % m_vel

end function

function particle_system_radius(this) result(arr)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    real(dp), pointer :: arr(:)

    arr => this % m_r

end function

function particle_system_count(this) result(count)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    integer :: count

    count = this % m_n_particles

end function

v0, rmin, rmax, and dt return the matching component. dt returns m_dt, and init never assigns m_dt, so a caller of dt() reads a component that this program never sets. The stepper does not call dt(). It computes a step from r_\min and v0v_0v0​ when the caller does not pass one.

set_rmin, set_rmax, and set_v0 store one number. They do not rebuild the arrays. The window does not call them. Update destroys the system and initializes a new one.

positions, velocities, and radius return pointers associated with the private arrays. The simulation writes through those pointers. The stepper is in the same module, so the private attribute still allows that write.

count returns m_n_particles.

particle_system_particle and particle_system_particle_count¶

particle_classes.f90
subroutine particle_system_particle(this, idx, x, y, r)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    integer, intent(in) :: idx
    real(dp), intent(out) :: x, y, r

    x = this % m_pos(idx, 1)
    y = this % m_pos(idx, 2)
    r = this % m_r(idx)

end subroutine

function particle_system_particle_count(this) result(count)

    class(ParticleSystem) :: this
    integer :: count

    count = size(this % m_pos, 1)

end function

particle copies xxx, yyy, and rrr for a 1-based index out through intent(out) arguments:

x=pi,1,y=pi,2,r=rix = p_{i,1}, \qquad y = p_{i,2}, \qquad r = r_ix=pi,1​,y=pi,2​,r=ri​
(6)

This is the procedure the paint loop calls. particle_count returns size(m_pos, 1), the allocated row count, rather than m_n_particles. After a normal init those two numbers match. After destroy, the arrays are gone and particle_count must not be called.

ParticleSimulation¶

particle_classes.f90
type ParticleSimulation
private
    class(ParticleSystem), pointer :: m_psys
contains
    procedure :: init              => particle_simulator_init
    procedure :: update            => particle_simulator_update
    procedure :: check_boundaries  => particle_simulator_check_boundaries
    procedure :: check_collisions  => particle_simulator_check_collisions
    procedure :: run               => particle_simulator_run
    procedure :: run_iteration     => particle_simulator_run_iteration
end type

The simulator holds one class(ParticleSystem) pointer. It does not own the particles. init saves the pointer the caller already allocated. The bindings are update, check_boundaries, check_collisions, run, and run_iteration.

particle_simulator_init¶

particle_classes.f90
subroutine particle_simulator_init(this, psys)

    class(ParticleSimulation) :: this
    class(ParticleSystem), pointer :: psys

    this % m_psys => psys

end subroutine particle_simulator_init

this % m_psys => psys stores the caller’s pointer. The simulator and the caller then name the same particle system.

particle_simulator_update¶

particle_classes.f90
subroutine particle_simulator_update(this, dtin)

    class(ParticleSimulation) :: this

    integer(ik) :: i
    real(dp), intent(in), optional :: dtin
    real(dp) :: dt
    real(dp), pointer :: pos(:,:)
    real(dp), pointer :: vel(:,:)
    real(dp), pointer :: r(:)

    pos => this % m_psys % positions()
    vel => this % m_psys % velocities()
    r => this % m_psys % radius()

    if (present(dtin)) then
            dt = dtin
    else
            dt = this % m_psys % rmin()/(10.0_dp*this % m_psys % v0())
    end if

    pos = pos + vel * dt

end subroutine particle_simulator_update

Reads positions, velocities, and radii through the accessors. The radius pointer r is fetched and never used. The index i is declared and never used.

If the caller passes dtin, that is the step. If not, the step is

Got function '\min' with no arguments as subscript at position 20: …ta t = \frac{r_\̲m̲i̲n̲}{10\, v_0}

\Delta t = \frac{r_\min}{10\, v_0}

dt = this % m_psys % rmin()/(10.0_dp*this % m_psys % v0()) is that quotient. With the defaults,

Δt=0.00510×0.001=0.5\Delta t = \frac{0.005}{10 \times 0.001} = 0.5Δt=10×0.0010.005​=0.5
(8)

The update itself is one array assignment, pos = pos + vel * dt, which is

p←p+v Δt\mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}\,\Delta tp←p+vΔt
(9)

A particle at speed 0.001 therefore moves

v0 Δt=0.001×0.5=5×10−4v_0\,\Delta t = 0.001 \times 0.5 = 5\times 10^{-4}v0​Δt=0.001×0.5=5×10−4
(10)

per step, in a square of side 1. The window never passes a step, so every frame uses this formula, including after you change the radii and click Update. Changing the radii changes r_\min in a new system, and the next default step changes with it. The speed stays 0.001, because the window has no control for v0v_0v0​.

particle_simulator_check_boundaries¶

particle_classes.f90
subroutine particle_simulator_check_boundaries(this)

    class(ParticleSimulation) :: this
    integer(ik) :: i
    real(dp), pointer :: pos(:,:)
    real(dp), pointer :: vel(:,:)
    real(dp), pointer :: r(:)

    pos => this % m_psys % positions()
    vel => this % m_psys % velocities()
    r => this % m_psys % radius()

    !associate (pos => this % m_psys % m_pos, vel => this % m_psys % m_vel, r => this % m_psys % m_r)

    do i=1,this % m_psys % count()
        if (pos(i,1) < r(i)) vel(i,1) = -vel(i,1)
        if (pos(i,1) > 1.0_dp-r(i)) vel(i,1) = -vel(i,1)
        if (pos(i,2) < r(i)) vel(i,2) = -vel(i,2)
        if (pos(i,2) > 1.0_dp-r(i)) vel(i,2) = -vel(i,2)
    end do

    !end associate

end subroutine

For each particle, if the center has crossed a wall by less than a radius, the matching velocity component is negated. The four tests are

x<r⇒vx←−vxx>1−r⇒vx←−vxy<r⇒vy←−vyy>1−r⇒vy←−vy\begin{aligned} x < r &\Rightarrow v_x \leftarrow -v_x \\ x > 1 - r &\Rightarrow v_x \leftarrow -v_x \\ y < r &\Rightarrow v_y \leftarrow -v_y \\ y > 1 - r &\Rightarrow v_y \leftarrow -v_y \end{aligned}x<rx>1−ry<ry>1−r​⇒vx​←−vx​⇒vx​←−vx​⇒vy​←−vy​⇒vy​←−vy​​
(11)

pos(i,1) < r(i) and the three lines after it are those four tests. The position is not assigned. A center that stays past the wall has its velocity flipped again on the next step, so a particle that has penetrated a wall can jitter. The test does not look at the sign of the velocity. The associate block is commented out. The live code uses the pointers from the three accessor calls.

particle_simulator_check_collisions¶

particle_classes.f90
subroutine particle_simulator_check_collisions(this)

    class(ParticleSimulation) :: this

    integer(ik) :: i, j
    real(dp) :: d, r1, r2
    real(dp) :: vi(2), vj(2)
    real(dp) :: si(2), sj(2)
    real(dp) :: n(2), vdiff(2)
    real(dp) :: q
    real(dp), pointer :: pos(:,:)
    real(dp), pointer :: vel(:,:)
    real(dp), pointer :: r(:)

    pos => this % m_psys % positions()
    vel => this % m_psys % velocities()
    r => this % m_psys % radius()


    !       | -------------|
    !               d
    ! | --- o --- |   | -- o -- |
    !          r1       r2
    !
    ! collide is true if d < (r1+r2)

    do i=1,this % m_psys % count()
        do j=i+1,this % m_psys % count()
            n = pos(j,:) - pos(i,:)
            d = sqrt( &
                (pos(j,1)-pos(i,1))**2.0_dp+ &
                (pos(j,2)-pos(i,2))**2)
            vdiff = vel(j,:) - vel(i,:)
            if ((d<(r(i)+r(j))).and.(dot_product(n,vdiff)<0.0_dp)) then
                q = dot_product(vdiff,n)/dot_product(n,n)
                vel(i,:) = vel(i,:) + n * q
                vel(j,:) = vel(j,:) - n * q
            endif
        end do
    end do

end subroutine

The nested loop compares each pair once, jjj from i+1i+1i+1 to the count. The comment sketches two circles of radii r1r_1r1​ and r2r_2r2​ whose centers are a distance ddd apart. The locals r1, r2, vi, vj, si, and sj are declared and never used. The radii actually used are r(i) and r(j).

For each pair the code builds

n=pj−pi,d=(xj−xi)2+(yj−yi)2,vdiff=vj−vi\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_i, \qquad d = \sqrt{(x_j-x_i)^2 + (y_j-y_i)^2}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{diff}} = \mathbf{v}_j - \mathbf{v}_in=pj​−pi​,d=(xj​−xi​)2+(yj​−yi​)2​,vdiff​=vj​−vi​
(12)

n = pos(j,:) - pos(i,:) is n\mathbf{n}n. The sqrt of the two squared differences is ddd, which is ∣n∣|\mathbf{n}|∣n∣. vdiff = vel(j,:) - vel(i,:) is the relative velocity of particle jjj as seen from particle iii.

A pair collides when the circles overlap and the particles are approaching:

d<ri+rjandn⋅vdiff<0d < r_i + r_j \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{diff}} < 0d<ri​+rj​andn⋅vdiff​<0
(13)

d<(r(i)+r(j)) and dot_product(n,vdiff)<0.0_dp are those two tests. The response assumes equal mass and exchanges the component of velocity along n\mathbf{n}n:

q=vdiff⋅nn⋅n,vi←vi+q n,vj←vj−q nq = \frac{\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{diff}}\cdot\mathbf{n}}{\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{n}}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_i \leftarrow \mathbf{v}_i + q\,\mathbf{n}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_j \leftarrow \mathbf{v}_j - q\,\mathbf{n}q=n⋅nvdiff​⋅n​,vi​←vi​+qn,vj​←vj​−qn
(14)

q = dot_product(vdiff,n)/dot_product(n,n) is the scalar. Adding n * q to vel(i,:) and subtracting it from vel(j,:) is the exchange. For equal mass, that swap is what an elastic collision does to the relative velocity along the line of centers: the normal component of vdiff\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{diff}}vdiff​ changes sign, and the tangential component is left alone.

The cost is the double loop. Five hundred particles are 500×499/2500 \times 499 / 2500×499/2 pairs on every frame, which is why the window’s timer makes the process busy.

particle_simulator_run and particle_simulator_run_iteration¶

particle_classes.f90
subroutine particle_simulator_run(this, n_iterations)

    class(ParticleSimulation) :: this
    integer, intent(in) :: n_iterations
    integer :: i

    call this % m_psys % write_sizes()

    do i = 1,n_iterations
        call this % check_collisions()
        call this % check_boundaries()
        call this % update()
        call this % m_psys % write_positions()
    end do

end subroutine

subroutine particle_simulator_run_iteration(this)

    class(ParticleSimulation) :: this

    call this % check_collisions()
    call this % check_boundaries()
    call this % update()

end subroutine

run writes the radius block once, then for each requested iteration checks collisions, checks walls, steps, and appends the positions. The console program calls run(1000).

run_iteration is one pass of the same three calls and does not touch particle.state. The timer calls this.

particle_interface¶

particle_interface.f90
module particle_interface

! ---- Interface class for the particle system classes.

use iso_c_binding
use mf_datatypes
use mf_utils
use particle_classes
use particle_utils

implicit none

! ---- Private instances of the the Fortran particle classes

class(ParticleSystem), private, pointer :: p_particle_system
class(ParticleSimulation), private, pointer:: p_particle_simulation

The module is the C API. Two module variables, p_particle_system and p_particle_simulation, are private polymorphic pointers. Every bind(C) procedure uses those two objects. There is one system in the process.

particle_intf_system_init¶

particle_interface.f90
subroutine particle_intf_system_init(n, min_radius, max_radius, v0) bind(C, name='particle_system_init')

    integer(c_int), value :: n
    real(c_double), value :: min_radius
    real(c_double), value :: max_radius
    real(c_double), value :: v0

    print*, 'Allocating particle system...'

    allocate(p_particle_system)
    allocate(p_particle_simulation)

    call p_particle_system % init(n, min_radius, max_radius, v0)
    call p_particle_simulation % init(p_particle_system)

end subroutine

The C name is particle_system_init. The Fortran name is particle_intf_system_init. n, min_radius, max_radius, and v0 all have value, so they match int and double parameters passed by value. The body prints Allocating particle system..., allocates both objects, and calls the type-bound init on each. When standard output is a terminal, that line shows up. When the GUI run that produced the recording redirected standard output to a file, the Fortran buffer was still holding the line at exit, so the saved GUI log did not contain it. The console driver does not go through this interface.

particle_intf_system_particle_params¶

particle_interface.f90
subroutine particle_intf_system_particle_params(min_radius, max_radius, v0) bind(C, name='particle_system_params')

    real(c_double), intent(out) :: min_radius
    real(c_double), intent(out) :: max_radius
    real(c_double), intent(out) :: v0

    min_radius = p_particle_system % rmin()
    max_radius = p_particle_system % rmax()
    v0 = p_particle_system % v0()

end subroutine

Copies r_\min, r_\max, and v0v_0v0​ out through intent(out) doubles. Those are pointers on the C side. paintEvent uses the two radii to scale the color. v0 is retrieved and the painter does not use it.

particle_intf_system_particle¶

particle_interface.f90
subroutine particle_intf_system_particle(idx, x, y, r) bind(C, name='particle_system_particle')

    integer(c_int), value :: idx
    real(c_double), intent(out) :: x, y, r

    call p_particle_system % particle(idx, x, y, r)

end subroutine

The Fortran arguments are idx, x, y, and r, with idx passed by value. The C header names the last pointer z.

particle_interface.h
extern "C" {

void particle_system_init(int n, double rmin, double rmax, double v0);
void particle_system_destroy();
void particle_system_run_iteration();
void particle_system_particle(int idx, double* x, double* y, double* z);
int particle_system_particle_count();
void particle_system_params(double* min_radius, double* max_radius, double* v0);

The value written through that pointer is the radius. The painter stores it in a variable named r and draws a circle. The header’s name z is the name of that radius pointer.

particle_intf_system_particle_count¶

particle_interface.f90
function particle_intf_system_particle_count() result(count) bind(C, name='particle_system_particle_count')

    integer(c_int) :: count

    count = p_particle_system % particle_count()

end function

Returns integer(c_int). The C header returns int. The body calls the type-bound particle_count.

particle_intf_system_run_iteration and particle_intf_system_destroy¶

particle_interface.f90
subroutine particle_intf_system_run_iteration() bind(C, name='particle_system_run_iteration')

    call p_particle_simulation % run_iteration()

end subroutine

subroutine particle_intf_system_destroy() bind(C, name='particle_system_destroy')

    print*, 'Deallocating particle system ...'

    deallocate(p_particle_simulation)
    deallocate(p_particle_system)

end subroutine

One calls run_iteration. The other prints Deallocating particle system ... and deallocates both pointers. The same buffering note applies to that print.

particle_interface.h

subroutine particle_intf_system_init(n) bind(C, name='init_particle_system')

The header also contains a block of Fortran, commented out with /* */. It is an older sketch of the interface, with different names and a fixed count of 1000. It is not compiled.

The C++ window¶

main¶

main.cpp
#include "mainwindow.h"

#include <QApplication>

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    QApplication a(argc, argv);
    MainWindow w;
    w.show();
    return a.exec();
}

main constructs a QApplication, a MainWindow, shows it, and enters the event loop. There is no particle code here. Building the window runs MainWindow’s constructor, and that constructor creates the Fortran system.

MainWindow¶

mainwindow.h
#ifndef MAINWINDOW_H
#define MAINWINDOW_H

#include <QMainWindow>

QT_BEGIN_NAMESPACE
namespace Ui { class MainWindow; }
QT_END_NAMESPACE

class MainWindow : public QMainWindow
{
    Q_OBJECT

private:
    int m_nParticles;
    double m_minRadius;
    double m_maxRadius;
    double m_v0;
    bool m_firstTime;
    double m_maxSize;

public:
    MainWindow(QWidget *parent = nullptr);
    ~MainWindow();

    void updateParams();
    void updateControls();

    void createParticleSystem();

private slots:
    void on_actionRun_triggered();
    void on_actionStop_triggered();
    void on_maxSizeSlider_valueChanged(int value);
    void on_actionUpdate_triggered();

private:
    Ui::MainWindow *ui;
};
#endif // MAINWINDOW_H

The members are the particle count, the two radii, m_v0, a m_firstTime flag, and m_maxSize. The slots follow the names of the actions and the slider, which is how Qt connects them.

mainwindow.cpp
MainWindow::MainWindow(QWidget *parent)
    : QMainWindow(parent)
    , ui(new Ui::MainWindow)
    , m_nParticles(500)
    , m_minRadius(0.005)
    , m_maxRadius(0.015)
    , m_v0(0.001)
    , m_firstTime(true)
    , m_maxSize(600.0)
{
    // Setup user interface from UI-description

    ui->setupUi(this);

    // Set default values for controls

    updateControls();

    // Create particle system

    createParticleSystem();
}

MainWindow::~MainWindow()
{
    // Delete particle system

    particle_system_destroy();

    // Delete user interface

    delete ui;
}

The constructor’s initializer list sets 500, 0.005, 0.015, 0.001, true, and 600. There is no widget for m_v0. Update cannot change the speed. It stays 0.001. The constructor calls setupUi, which is generated from mainwindow.ui, then updateControls, then createParticleSystem. The destructor calls particle_system_destroy and deletes the generated UI object.

mainwindow.cpp
void MainWindow::updateParams()
{
    // Update parameters from controls

    bool ok;
    m_nParticles = ui->particleSpin->value();

    auto minRadius = ui->minRadiusText->text().toDouble(&ok);
    if (ok) m_minRadius = minRadius;

    auto maxRadius = ui->maxRadiusText->text().toDouble(&ok);
    if (ok) m_maxRadius = maxRadius;

    // Set updated values in the controls

    updateControls();
}

void MainWindow::updateControls()
{
    // Update controls with values

    ui->particleSpin->setValue(m_nParticles);
    ui->minRadiusText->setText(QString::number(m_minRadius));
    ui->maxRadiusText->setText(QString::number(m_maxRadius));
    ui->maxSizeSlider->setValue(int(m_maxSize));
}

updateParams reads the spin box into m_nParticles. It parses the two radius fields with toDouble. A field that does not parse is left unchanged, because ok is tested before the assignment. It does not read a speed. It finishes by writing the members back into the widgets, so a rejected parse snaps the text back to the old value.

updateControls is that write-back: the spin box, both radius fields, and the slider. The slider value is int(m_maxSize).

mainwindow.cpp
void MainWindow::createParticleSystem()
{
    // Stop timer updates

    ui->drawingArea->stopSimulation();

    // If not first time destroy current particle system

    if (!m_firstTime)
        particle_system_destroy();

    // Create particle system

    particle_system_init(m_nParticles, m_minRadius, m_maxRadius, m_v0);

    m_firstTime = false;

    // Start simulation

    ui->drawingArea->runSimulation();
}

void MainWindow::on_actionRun_triggered()
{
    ui->drawingArea->runSimulation();
}


void MainWindow::on_actionStop_triggered()
{
    ui->drawingArea->stopSimulation();
}

void MainWindow::on_maxSizeSlider_valueChanged(int value)
{
    ui->drawingArea->setMaxSize(double(value));
}


void MainWindow::on_actionUpdate_triggered()
{
    // Handling a click on the Update button

    updateParams();
    createParticleSystem();
}

createParticleSystem stops the timer, destroys the Fortran system unless this is the first call, calls particle_system_init with the four members, clears m_firstTime, and starts the timer.

on_actionRun_triggered starts the timer. on_actionStop_triggered stops it. The toolbar text for that action is Pause. The name actionStop is the object name in the .ui file. Qt connects the action to the slot by that name because the slot follows the pattern on_<object>_<signal>.

on_maxSizeSlider_valueChanged passes the integer to ParticleCanvas::setMaxSize. Dragging the slider rescales the drawing on the next paint. It does not rebuild the particles and it does not change a Fortran value.

on_actionUpdate_triggered runs updateParams and createParticleSystem. That is the button in the recording. The fields were set to 80, 0.012, and 0.040, and Update constructed a new system with those numbers.

The window description puts the controls in a row and the canvas under them.

File → New and File → Open are actions in the menu. No slot is connected to them. Choosing them does nothing. Run, Pause, and Update are on the toolbar. The canvas is a promoted widget: uic turns ParticleCanvas and the header particle_canvas.h into the member ui->drawingArea.

ParticleCanvas¶

particle_canvas.h
#ifndef PARTICLECANVAS_H
#define PARTICLECANVAS_H

#include <QWidget>
#include <QTimer>
#include <QBrush>
#include <QPen>

class ParticleCanvas : public QWidget
{
    Q_OBJECT
private:
    QTimer* m_timer;
    double m_maxSize;

public:
    explicit ParticleCanvas(QWidget *parent = nullptr);

    void paintEvent(QPaintEvent *);

    void setMaxSize(double maxSize);

    void runSimulation();
    void stopSimulation();


signals:


public slots:

    void on_timer_update();
};

#endif // PARTICLECANVAS_H

The canvas is a QWidget. Q_OBJECT is what moc looks for. m_maxSize is the slider’s scale, in pixels, of the unit square.

particle_canvas.cpp
ParticleCanvas::ParticleCanvas(QWidget *parent)
    : QWidget{parent}
    , m_maxSize(600.0)
{
    // Create timer for repeatly redrawing particle system

    m_timer = new QTimer(this);

    // Connect timer signal to on_timer_update()

    connect(m_timer, SIGNAL(timeout()), this, SLOT(on_timer_update()));
}

The constructor creates a QTimer owned by the widget and connects timeout() to on_timer_update(). The connection uses the SIGNAL / SLOT macros. m_maxSize starts at 600, the same default as the window.

particle_canvas.cpp
void ParticleCanvas::paintEvent(QPaintEvent *)
{
    QPainter painter(this);
    painter.setRenderHint(QPainter::Antialiasing, true);

    // Clear background

    painter.setPen(Qt::blue);
    painter.setBrush(Qt::black);
    painter.drawRect(0,0,this->width(), this->height());

    // Get number of particles

    auto count = particle_system_particle_count();

    painter.setBrush(Qt::white);
    painter.setPen(Qt::white);

    double x, y, r;
    double c;
    double rmin, rmax, v0;

    // Get rmin and rmax parameters

    particle_system_params(&rmin, &rmax, &v0);

    // Loop for drawing all particles

    for (auto i=1; i<=count; i++)
    {
        // Get particle position and size

        particle_system_particle(i, &x, &y, &r);

        // Draw particles

        c = 255.0 * (r - rmin) / (rmax - rmin);
        painter.setBrush((QBrush(QColor(255, 255, int(c)))));
        painter.setPen((QPen(QColor(255, 255, int(c)))));
        painter.drawEllipse(QPointF(width()/2.0 - m_maxSize/2.0 + x*m_maxSize, height()/2.0 -m_maxSize/2.0 + y*m_maxSize), r*m_maxSize, r*m_maxSize);
    }
}

paintEvent fills the widget with a black rectangle and a blue pen, asks Fortran for the count and the radius limits, and draws each particle from index 1 through count. Fortran arrays are 1-based, so the loop starts at 1.

The color channel is

Got function '\min' with no arguments as subscript at position 22: …5\,\frac{r - r_\̲m̲i̲n̲}{r_\max - r_\m…

c = 255\,\frac{r - r_\min}{r_\max - r_\min}

c = 255.0 * (r - rmin) / (rmax - rmin) is that quotient. Red and green stay at 255, and int(c) is the blue channel. A radius equal to r_\min gives c=0c = 0c=0, so the color is QColor(255, 255, 0), yellow. A radius equal to r_\max gives c=255c = 255c=255, so the color is QColor(255, 255, 255), white.

The circle is centered at

(w2−s2+xs,  h2−s2+ys)\left(\frac{w}{2} - \frac{s}{2} + x s,\; \frac{h}{2} - \frac{s}{2} + y s\right)(2w​−2s​+xs,2h​−2s​+ys)
(16)

with radius rsr srs, where sss is m_maxSize and (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) is the Fortran position in the unit square. The drawEllipse call is those two expressions: width()/2.0 - m_maxSize/2.0 + x*m_maxSize and the same form for height() and y, and both radii are r*m_maxSize. Dragging the slider to the right increases sss, so the same unit square is drawn across more pixels and the disks grow. That is the slider motion in the clip.

particle_canvas.cpp
void ParticleCanvas::setMaxSize(double maxSize)
{
    m_maxSize = maxSize;
}

void ParticleCanvas::runSimulation()
{
    // Start timer

    m_timer->start();
}

void ParticleCanvas::stopSimulation()
{
    // Stop timer

    m_timer->stop();
}

void ParticleCanvas::on_timer_update()
{
    particle_system_run_iteration();
    this->repaint();
}

setMaxSize stores the slider value. The next paintEvent uses it.

runSimulation calls m_timer->start() with no interval. A QTimer started that way uses an interval of 0 and fires whenever the event loop is idle. The window therefore steps the particles as fast as the collision loop and the paint allow. stopSimulation stops the timer. Pause in the recording is that call. The frames sit still while the timer is stopped, which is why the pointer can edit the fields without the collision loop eating the clicks.

on_timer_update calls particle_system_run_iteration and then repaint().

The console driver¶

main.f90 is a second program in the same directory. It is not in the CMake target. PROJECT_SOURCES lists the Fortran modules and the C++ window, and it does not list main.f90. Building the window does not build this driver.

main.f90
program myfortran

use mf_datatypes
use particle_classes

implicit none

class(ParticleSystem), pointer :: p_particle_system
class(ParticleSimulation), pointer:: p_particle_simulation

allocate(p_particle_system)
allocate(p_particle_simulation)

call p_particle_system % init(1000)
call p_particle_simulation % init(p_particle_system)

call p_particle_simulation % run(1000)

deallocate(p_particle_simulation)
deallocate(p_particle_system)

contains

end program myfortran

It allocates a system and a simulation on polymorphic pointers, initializes 1000 particles with the default radii and speed, and calls run(1000). There is no print. Standard output is empty. The result is the file particle.state in the working directory.

Compiled and run on this machine:

$ gfortran -O2 -c mf_datatypes.f90 mf_utils.f90 particle_utils.f90 particle_classes.f90 main.f90
$ gfortran -O2 -o particle_console mf_datatypes.o mf_utils.o particle_utils.o particle_classes.o main.o

The run took 2 seconds. particle.state is 24 MB and 1,002,001 lines. The first line of the radius block is the count 1000, then one radius per line. Each of the 1000 iterations appends the count and 1000 position lines. The line count is

1001+1000×1001=10020011001 + 1000 \times 1001 = 10020011001+1000×1001=1002001
(17)

The coordinates are one draw of the random generator. A second run will not match them.

The excerpt is the start of the radius block, the start of the first position block, and the last three lines of the file.

CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.5)

project(cpp_fortran VERSION 0.1 LANGUAGES CXX C Fortran)

set(CMAKE_INCLUDE_CURRENT_DIR ON)

set(CMAKE_AUTOUIC ON)

        main.cpp

)

if(${QT_VERSION_MAJOR} GREATER_EQUAL 6)
    qt_add_executable(cpp_fortran
        MANUAL_FINALIZATION

    )
# Define target properties for Android with Qt 6 as:

else()

        add_library(cpp_fortran SHARED
            ${PROJECT_SOURCES}
        )
# Define properties for Android with Qt 5 after find_package() calls as:
#    set(ANDROID_PACKAGE_SOURCE_DIR "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/android")
    else()
        add_executable(cpp_fortran
            ${PROJECT_SOURCES}
        )
    endif()
endif()

target_link_libraries(cpp_fortran PRIVATE Qt${QT_VERSION_MAJOR}::Widgets)

set_target_properties(cpp_fortran PROPERTIES
    MACOSX_BUNDLE_GUI_IDENTIFIER my.example.com
    MACOSX_BUNDLE_BUNDLE_VERSION ${PROJECT_VERSION}
    MACOSX_BUNDLE_SHORT_VERSION_STRING ${PROJECT_VERSION_MAJOR}.${PROJECT_VERSION_MINOR}
    MACOSX_BUNDLE TRUE
    WIN32_EXECUTABLE TRUE
)

install(TARGETS cpp_fortran
    BUNDLE DESTINATION .
    LIBRARY DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR})

if(QT_VERSION_MAJOR EQUAL 6)
    qt_finalize_executable(cpp_fortran)
endif()

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.5) is the version the list was written for. CMake 3.31 on this machine still configures it. project enables C, C++, and Fortran. The C compiler is detected because Qt’s own checks use it. None of this project’s sources are C.

CMAKE_AUTOUIC, CMAKE_AUTOMOC, and CMAKE_AUTORCC are the three generators. CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17 matches the language Qt 6 headers use. find_package(QT NAMES Qt6 Qt5 ...) and the following find_package(Qt${QT_VERSION_MAJOR} ...) are the usual Qt 5-or-6 form. On this machine that resolved to Qt 6.8.2 Widgets.

qt_add_executable is the Qt 6 way to build the program. The else branch is the Qt 5 form, and it was not taken. target_link_libraries attaches Qt6::Widgets, which brings Qt6::Gui, Qt6::Core, and the OpenGL libraries those targets need. The bundle and install lines are for macOS and for cmake --install. The recording did not install anything. It ran the binary from the build directory.

main.f90 is absent from PROJECT_SOURCES. particle_interface.h is listed so the build rebuilds when the C prototypes change.

The link line is /usr/bin/c++ plus the Qt libraries, -lgfortran, and -lquadmath. That is the same reason as in the small Fortran-calls-C++ program: the driver is the C++ compiler, and the Fortran runtime is an extra library. The rpath points at the Qt 6 library directory so the dynamic loader finds libQt6Widgets.so.6 when the binary starts.
